prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us ranked GLP-1 first, which is notable, but agreement on ranking is not the argument. The argument is the unbroken arc from gut-hormone physiology (proglucagon processing, the incretin effect, GLP-1 as an insulinotropic and satiety signal, the truncated active form) to drugs with large, independently replicated outcome trials in type 2 diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal disease. Originality, clarity, durability and impact are all strong, and the evidence base is mature enough that recognition is timely rather than speculative. A prize built on Holst (physiology of secretion and action), Drucker (receptor and proglucagon-peptide biology, translation) and Mojsov (identification of the active peptide) rewards the discovery side, which is where a Medicine prize is most defensible, and keeps the industrial chemistry out of the credited trio.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is publicly contested, and Habener and others are not among the credited names, so any trio omits someone with a credible claim. Knudsen's long-acting analogue chemistry is what actually delivered the drugs patients take, and a prize that leaves her out can be read as honouring the idea but not the medicine. If the committee concludes that credit for the active peptide cannot be adjudicated with confidence, the configuration is weaker than it looks and B001 or B035, which have their own allocation problems, are not obviously better.

responses.point: Sandberg proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for B002 and left Mojsov out only because of the three-person limit, describing the arc from peptide biology to long-acting analogues as a coherent unit.
responses.response: I take the point that Knudsen's work is why the drugs work as medicines, and that is the strongest case for her. I still prefer Mojsov because identification of the active peptide is a discovery contribution, whereas long-acting analogue design is development that the prize would honour only by changing its framing from discovery to translation. I would not call that a settled disagreement. If the committee is not confident about Mojsov's priority, I would reconsider and accept Knudsen in that slot, but I would want the citation to say plainly which framing we have chosen.

responses.point: Perlmann regards Holst, Drucker and Mojsov as the strongest scientific contributors, argues Knudsen's industrial work can be left out, and notes that the list may omit people with decisive contributions.
responses.response: I agree with the core trio, and his caution about omissions is the one that bothers me most. I do not think we can fix it by adding names, because the cap is three. We can only state the citation narrowly enough that it claims what these three did, so that Habener and others are not implicitly written out. I would also be wary of treating his comment about industrial work as a settled reason to exclude Knudsen, since the committee has to defend that exclusion on its merits.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks optogenetics second and treats the three-name limit as forcing a judgement call between Nagel and Hegemann on the channel and Boyden and Deisseroth on neuronal use.
responses.response: I agree optogenetics is a strong second, and I put it there too, but I am less comfortable than he seems to be with it as a prize. Six credible names, a priority dispute over the first neuronal demonstration, and no clean three-way split make it harder to defend than GLP-1. I also disagree with the idea that a tool's breadth of use can substitute for a medical consequence. I would accept it because of its exceptional impact on experimental neuroscience, not because attribution is clearer than it is, and I would want the committee to say how it weighs a method against a therapy before choosing it.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius notes the gap in the CAR-T credit, since Eshhar's original chimeric receptor concept is not among the supplied names, but still ranks it third for its durable remissions.
responses.response: I share her concern and think it is the main reason I rank B035 below optogenetics as a configuration, despite the clinical effect. A trio of June, Sadelain and Rosenberg risks crediting clinical proof while omitting the origin of the concept. I would only support it if the committee can articulate a citation that fits what these three did, and I am not sure that Rosenberg's role fits comfortably beside the CAR designers.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's contribution to identifying the active GLP-1 peptide can be defended against competing claims, and whether Knudsen should take that place instead.
Whether a citation can be worded to credit discovery without implicitly excluding Habener and others outside the credited names.
Whether the committee prefers a single achievement or a two-part prize, given that every strong alternative also has crowded attribution.
Long-term safety and durability of benefit for incretin therapies are still being characterised.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with the preferred configuration is apparent from my profile: none of Drucker, Holst or Mojsov is documented as a collaborator or colleague. My profile records roughly twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann (dopamine neurons, Nurr1), but he is not a candidate, so no recusal issue arises. My Rockefeller postdoc with Paul Greengard is also unrelated to any shortlisted candidate. My neuroscience background touches B001 and B047 only by topic, which I try to discount.
